title: How Much of Remote Work Is Actually Run by AI Now?
content:
Screenshot of anthropic.com (source)

How Much of Remote Work Is Actually Run by AI Now?

My view (an opinion, not a measured result): AI is heavily used for documentation-style tasks such as notes, summaries, first drafts and status updates, and I'd expect people to keep ownership of most judgment calls. The studies cited below measure Claude.ai and Claude API usage, not all remote work, so they cannot give a total share of remote work that AI runs. Any claim like "AI runs half of remote work" needs a definition of "runs" and a measured sample.

What's Actually Going On

Screenshot of anthropic.com (source)

Anthropic's usage data is mixed on augmentation versus automation

Anthropic publishes an ongoing Economic Index based on usage of Claude. It covers Claude.ai and Anthropic's first-party API, not all remote work, and Anthropic notes that Claude is used for work that is not broadly representative of the US economy. In January 2025, 56% of Claude.ai conversations were classified as augmentation versus 41% automation; by August 2025, more conversations were classified as automated than augmented (January 2026 report). In the March 2026 report (February 2026 sample), augmentation on Claude.ai increased slightly, while automation decreased sharply in the first-party API data (March 2026 report).

Translation: the split on Claude.ai has been close and has moved over time, so these data don't show a steady move in one direction. They describe how Claude is used, not whether jobs are being replaced.

The API side is a different animal entirely

Where businesses wire AI directly into their systems, Anthropic describes API use as automation-dominant. Anthropic reported that Office and Administrative Support tasks rose 3 percentage points to 13% of API transcripts by November 2025, and because API use is automation-dominant, this suggests businesses are increasingly automating routine back-office workflows like email management, document processing, CRM, and scheduling.

The specific workflows spreading fastest are telling. Anthropic flagged two API workflows whose shares at least doubled in three months: business sales and outreach automation - lead qualification research, customer data enrichment, cold-email drafting - and automated trading and market ops. These are task categories whose share of sampled API traffic grew; the report does not measure effects on headcount.

Coding is still the deep end

Coding remains the most common use, with Computer and Mathematical occupation tasks accounting for 35% of Claude.ai conversations - though between November 2025 and February 2026 usage became less concentrated, with the top 10 most common tasks falling from 24% of conversations to 19%. Software-related tasks remain the largest share of sampled Claude.ai conversations in the February 2026 sample, though the report found use cases diversifying. That is a statement about Claude.ai usage, not about all remote work.

Distribution is what makes this feel sudden

One reason AI can feel more present at work, in my view, is bundling. Zoom announced in 2023 that AI Companion would be available at no additional cost for customers with paid services in their Zoom user accounts (its footnote says availability may vary for select verticals and regions; Zoom announcement). When meeting AI becomes a checkbox inside a subscription you already pay for, adoption stops being a decision and becomes a default. That makes "is your team using AI?" a less useful question than "for what, and with what review?" (my view).

Geography shows some convergence within the US. From August 2025 to February 2026, the share of per-person Claude usage going to the top five US states fell from 30% to 24%. Anthropic says US convergence continued but at a slower pace, and that across countries usage became slightly more concentrated.

My Take

Screenshot of anthropic.com (source)

The framing "how much of remote work is run by AI" is the wrong unit of measurement, and that's why every answer you've read feels either wildly overstated or uselessly cautious.

Here's how I'd actually carve it up. Remote work has three layers:

  1. The documentation layer - notes, summaries, recaps, status updates, meeting minutes, first-pass drafts, ticket descriptions. In my view, AI is used heavily here; the studies cited above don't measure how much of this material humans edit.
  2. The production layer - code, decks, analyses, outreach sequences, support replies. AI drafts, a human approves. This is the contested middle, and it's where the augmentation-to-automation shift the Economic Index keeps tracking is actually playing out.
  3. The judgment layer - what to build, who to hire, which client to fire, whether a number is wrong. I'd expect humans to keep ownership of most of these decisions, but that is my judgment, not a measured figure.

My concern with headline percentages: averaging these three layers into one number can hide more than it shows. A statement like "AI does 30% of work" would, in my opinion, understate layer one and overstate layer three.

A second opinion: automation isn't necessarily the scary endpoint, and augmentation isn't necessarily the safe one. The automated work Anthropic describes, such as document processing, scheduling and lead enrichment, is routine. The layer I'd watch is layer two, where I worry that drafts good enough to approve quickly could let review quality slip; the studies cited here don't measure that.

To the skeptical reader who says this is overblown: I'd point at the API data, not the chat data. Chat usage is visible and feels incremental. API usage sits inside products and internal tooling, where users may not see it, and Anthropic's samples show workflows such as lead qualification, data enrichment and cold-email drafting being automated through the API.

To the reader who says AI already runs everything: Anthropic's API data describes some workflows, such as outreach and market-monitoring tasks, being automated, but none of the studies cited here measures how much of remote work as a whole is run end to end by AI.

The Strongest Counterargument

Screenshot of news.zoom.com (source)

The fairest objection to my position is that usage telemetry from one AI vendor is not the economy. Anthropic itself is careful about this: its March 2026 report says Claude is used for high-value, complex work that is not broadly representative of the US economy, and that adoption is uneven (more intense in high-income countries and in US places with more knowledge workers). Claude users are not a random sample of workers. Even in the very first Economic Index, AI use was more prevalent for mid-to-high-wage occupations like programmers and data scientists, and lower at both the bottom and top of the pay scale.

So yes: my view of the documentation layer is an opinion that probably fits knowledge-work-heavy, laptop-first companies best, and may fit a remote claims processor at a regional insurer less well.

I still land roughly where I land, but the data are mixed: Claude.ai use diversified, US state-level usage converged more slowly, and some API workflows doubled in share. What these studies can't tell us is how far this extends across remote work as a whole.

Bottom Line

Who should care: anyone whose remote job is mostly producing documents about work rather than doing the work.

What to actually do:

  • Audit your week by layer, not by tool. If more than half your hours land in layer one, in my view that may be an exposure rather than a productivity win waiting to happen.
  • Stop paying for AI you already own. Bundled AI in conferencing and office suites may overlap with standalone note-takers. Check what's included before you renew a second subscription.
  • Move up a layer deliberately. In my view, a durable skill is being able to tell when confident-sounding output is wrong.
  • If you manage people: protect the junior pipeline. Routine tasks that AI tools handle well are often tasks people used to learn judgment on (my opinion).

FAQ

Is AI replacing remote jobs or just remote tasks? These data describe tasks, not employment. Anthropic's usage reports track what Claude is used for and cannot show whether jobs are being replaced.

Which remote work is most AI-run right now? In Anthropic's samples, software-related tasks are the largest share of Claude.ai conversations, and office and administrative support reached 13% of API transcripts. These samples do not cover all remote work. Computer and Mathematical tasks account for 35% of Claude.ai conversations , and Office and Administrative Support reached 13% of API transcripts by November 2025 .

Do I need to pay for AI meeting tools? Probably not as a separate line item. Zoom includes AI Companion at no additional cost with paid Zoom user accounts . Zoom's announcement notes that availability may vary by region and vertical. Buy a dedicated tool only if you have a real gap the bundled version can't cover.

Will AI usage keep spreading outside tech hubs? Within the US, per-person Claude usage has been converging, though more slowly than before. The top five US states' share of per-person usage dropped from 30% to 24% between August 2025 and February 2026, and Anthropic notes that across countries, usage became slightly more concentrated.

Correction note (October 2026): This post was revised to remove augmentation/automation ratios I could not confirm in Anthropic's reports (keeping the dated 56% vs 41% January 2025 figures), remove a layoffs-rate sentence that I could not find in Anthropic's reports, correct the claim that all measured series point toward more automation, and state clearly that the cited studies measure Claude usage and not all remote work. Sources: Anthropic Economic Index, January 2026, Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026, Zoom.
